items.title: Jamey Aebersold interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 26, 2022
items.q: Gene Perla, the bass player, did that. He and his friend. And they did it with half a dozen, six, seven, eight of my play-a-longs.

ctx.x: So the accompaniments that came with the book that’s over my shoulder, you took them and digitally they were able to be slowed down, is that correct?

Yeah. Gene Perla, the bass player, did that. He and his friend. And they did it with half a dozen, six, seven, eight of my play-a-longs. And the ones that were rushing a little bit, he straightened them out. I can remember playing with Volume 34 like “Just Friends” [scats]

and then it gets a little faster after a couple of minutes, then it gets a little faster. But now when I play with it I’m waiting for it to speed up and it doesn’t. It stays the same, which is nice of course.

items.title: Aebersold Jamey — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So we’ve been able to digitally have Gene Perla, the bass player, up in Easton, Pennsylvania, with his program that he’s got... It’s fantastic.

ctx.x: There you’ve got Volume 6 with Charlie Parker, and then Miles Davis, Sonny Rollins and Woody Shaw.

Incidentally, the Volume 1, the Volume 3, the Volume 6... Volume 14—Benny Golson. Volume 17—Horace Silver. Volume 18—Horace Silver. We, as of the last year or two...we have slowed those records down, those Play-A-Longs, and now they have two CDs— slower tempos and original tempos. Because jazz education has moved through the years down and down age-wise, so you’ve got 10-, 11- and 12-, 13-year-old people trying to play Volume 1, our Charlie Parker tunes, our Horace Silver tunes. So we’ve been able to digitally…
And was it pitch control...not pitch control...
